title: Toeplitz Matrix
description: Brute force to optimized: explicitly tracing every diagonal versus a single-pass local check against each cell's upper-left neighbor.

blocks.text: Given an m x n matrix matrix, return true if it is a TOEPLITZ MATRIX: every diagonal running from top-left to bottom-right has all the same elements.

blocks.caption: A single pass checks every cell against its immediate upper-left neighbor

blocks.text: Given a matrix, check whether every diagonal running from its top-left to its bottom-right direction consists of entirely identical values.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking a Repeating Wallpaper Pattern for Consistency
blocks.text: Like checking a grid of wallpaper tiles for a diagonally repeating pattern, where every tile should exactly match the tile diagonally above and to its left. Rather than tracing out each full diagonal stripe of tiles from one end to the other, simply checking every single tile against its one immediate upper-left neighbor is enough: if every such pair matches, the entire diagonal must be constant by simple chaining, since each tile links directly to the one before it.

blocks.caption: Checking only immediate upper-left neighbors is equivalent to checking whole diagonals, by chaining

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Every cell matches its upper-left neighbor: e.g., matrix[1][1]=1 matches matrix[0][0]=1; matrix[2][2]=1 matches matrix[1][1]=1","Every diagonal is constant","Tracing any diagonal confirms all its values are identical"],["Answer","true","The matrix is Toeplitz"]]}

blocks.text: Before explicitly tracing out every individual diagonal from its starting point to check that all its values match, notice that a purely local, pairwise check achieves the exact same result.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A diagonal running top-left to bottom-right consists of cells (i, j), (i+1, j+1), (i+2, j+2), and so on, where every consecutive pair of cells along it differs by exactly (+1, +1) in position.

Observation 2: If every cell matches the cell immediately diagonally above-left of it (matrix[i][j] == matrix[i-1][j-1]) for every valid (i, j), then by simple chaining, every cell along any given diagonal must equal every other cell on that same diagonal, since each one matches its immediate predecessor.

Observation 3: This means the ENTIRE diagonal-constant property can be verified with a single, purely local check at every cell, without ever needing to know which diagonal a cell belongs to or trace it out explicitly.

Observation 4: A single pass over all cells (i, j) with i >= 1 and j >= 1, checking matrix[i][j] against matrix[i-1][j-1], is both necessary and sufficient to confirm the whole matrix is Toeplitz.

Recognizing that a GLOBAL structural property (whole diagonals being constant) reduces to a simple LOCAL pairwise check (adjacent diagonal neighbors matching) is what avoids ever needing to trace out and store entire diagonals.
This is a local-implies-global reduction: checking only immediate diagonal neighbors is provably equivalent to checking whole diagonals, thanks to the transitive chaining of equality.
For every diagonal (identified by its starting cell along the top row or left column), explicitly walk it from start to end, checking that every value matches the first.

items: For every possible diagonal starting point (every cell in the first column, and every cell in the first row except the corner, to avoid double-counting), walk that diagonal from start to end.
While walking, compare every cell's value to the diagonal's very first value; if any mismatch is found, the matrix is not Toeplitz.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Diagonals are enumerated by their starting cell: every row in the first column, plus every column in the first row except the very corner (already covered by the first loop), covering every diagonal exactly once.
checkDiagonal walks its diagonal fully from the given start, comparing every subsequent cell against the diagonal's own first value.
The function returns false the instant any mismatch is found along any diagonal, short-circuiting further checking.

blocks.text: Every diagonal is explicitly traced and validated in full, so the correct answer is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), since every cell is visited exactly once across all the diagonal walks combined (each cell belongs to exactly one diagonal).
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: explicitly identifying diagonal starting points and walking each one separately adds unnecessary bookkeeping, when a single direct pass comparing every cell to its immediate upper-left neighbor achieves the exact same validation.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force explicitly enumerates and walks every diagonal from its starting point. Instead, recognize that checking every cell against its immediate upper-left neighbor (matrix[i][j] == matrix[i-1][j-1]) is exactly equivalent to the whole-diagonal-constant property, by simple transitive chaining. A single nested loop over all cells with i >= 1 and j >= 1 suffices, with no need to track which diagonal any given cell belongs to.

For every cell (i, j) with i from 1 to rows-1 and j from 1 to cols-1, check whether matrix[i][j] equals matrix[i-1][j-1]. If any pair doesn't match, return false immediately. If every pair matches, return true.
Check every cell against its immediate upper-left diagonal neighbor in a single, direct pass.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Every cell matches its upper-left neighbor, so the answer is true, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), visiting every eligible cell exactly once, with early exit on the first mismatch found.
Space: O(1) extra.

If matrix[i][j] equals matrix[i-1][j-1] for EVERY valid (i, j), then following any diagonal from its starting cell forward, each step confirms the next cell equals the previous one, and by simple transitivity, every cell along that diagonal must be equal to the diagonal's first value. Conversely, if the matrix truly is Toeplitz, every such local pair trivially matches, since they lie on the same constant diagonal. The local check and the global property are therefore exactly equivalent.

items: The loop bounds (i, j starting at 1) naturally skip the first row and first column, since those cells have no upper-left neighbor to compare against.
The comparison is purely local, requiring no knowledge of which diagonal a given cell belongs to.
The function returns false immediately upon the first mismatch, avoiding unnecessary further comparisons.

blocks.text: Recognizing that a global structural property (every diagonal being constant) reduces to a simple local pairwise check (matching immediate diagonal neighbors) via transitive chaining is a broadly useful simplification technique.

items: Explicitly tracing out and storing full diagonals when a much simpler local check suffices.
Comparing a cell to the wrong neighbor (e.g., matrix[i-1][j] or matrix[i][j-1], which check row/column consistency, not diagonal consistency).
Forgetting to skip the first row and first column, which have no valid upper-left neighbor to compare against.

items: Explicitly state and justify the local-implies-global reduction (why checking immediate upper-left neighbors alone is sufficient) before coding, since this insight is the entire crux of an efficient solution here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Every diagonal must satisfy some constant/consistent property" points toward reducing the check to comparing each cell against its immediate diagonal neighbor, relying on transitive chaining rather than tracing full diagonals explicitly.

items: How would you handle this if the matrix were given as a stream of rows (not all available in memory at once)? Only the immediately previous row ever needs to be kept in memory, since each cell only ever needs to compare against the row directly above it.
How would you check anti-diagonals (top-right to bottom-left) instead? The same local-check idea applies, but comparing matrix[i][j] to matrix[i-1][j+1] instead.

What if the matrix had missing (unknown) values that could be filled in to make it Toeplitz? This becomes a constraint-satisfaction problem: group cells by diagonal, and check that every diagonal's known values (if any) agree, then any unknowns could be filled with that diagonal's established value.

A local-implies-global structural check, conceptually related to Matrix Diagonal Sum's direct index-formula thinking, but here reducing a whole-diagonal-consistency check to a single adjacent-pair comparison instead of summing specific known positions.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(rows * cols) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (local upper-left neighbor check): O(rows * cols) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Local-implies-global reduction: checking immediate diagonal neighbors instead of tracing whole diagonals
Core Idea: Every diagonal is constant if and only if every cell equals the cell diagonally above-left of it, by transitive chaining
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A global "whole diagonal is constant" property reduces to a simple local pairwise check, with no need to trace or track diagonal membership
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: matrix[i][j] == matrix[i-1][j-1] for every valid cell
